title: Our Father God! Not Face to Face
description: Our Father God! Not Face to Face in Tonic Solfa to HIGHER GROUND, doh is G: the solfa with the words, staff notation, 3 verses and a piano.
about: Edwin Hubbell Chapin wrote these words. They were printed in the supplement of the 1866 edition of A Book of Hymns for Public and Private Devotion, compiled by Samuel Longfellow and Samuel Johnson (Boston, 1866), as hymn 487, “The Gate of Heaven”.

The book printed the words without tunes, marked Long Metre Double (8.8.8.8.8.8.8.8), to be sung to any tune of that metre. This page sets them to HIGHER GROUND; any other Long Metre Double tune fits them as well.
underlay: Our Fa-ther God! not face to face May mor-tal sense com-mune with Thee, Nor lift the cur-tains of that place Where dwells Thy se-cret Maj-es-ty. Yet whe-re-so'er our spi-rits bend In rev'-rent faith and hum-ble prayer, Thy pro-mised bless-ing will de-scend, And we shall find Thy spir-it there.

lines: Our Father God! not face to face
May mortal sense commune with Thee,
Nor lift the curtains of that place
Where dwells Thy secret Majesty.
Yet whereso'er our spirits bend
In rev'rent faith and humble prayer,
Thy promised blessing will descend,
And we shall find Thy spirit there.
Lord! be the spot where now we meet
An open gateway into heaven;
Here may we sit at Jesus' feet,
And feel our deepest sins forgiven.
Here may desponding care look up;
And sorrow lay its burden down,
Or learn, of him, to drink the cup,
To bear the cross, and win the crown.
Here may the sick and wandering soul
To truth still blind, to sin a slave,
Find better than Bethesda's pool,
Or than Siloam's healing wave.
And may we learn, while here apart
From the world's passion and its strife;
That Thy true shrine's a loving heart,
And Thy best praise a holy life!

source: A Book of Hymns for Public and Private Devotion (1848)
licence: Public domain: Edwin Hubbell Chapin died in 1880.
credits: Words by Edwin Hubbell Chapin (1814–1880), public domain, as printed in A Book of Hymns for Public and Private Devotion (1866); set to HIGHER GROUND by NoteFusion, as words-only hymn books were sung.
